system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2146-12-30 15:05:00 to 2147-01-08 17:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition, and congenital long QT syndrome, was admitted for abdominal pain and acute-on-chronic diarrhea. He reported symptoms similar to prior C. difficile infection. CT scan showed no obstruction or colitis, but stool testing confirmed C. difficile with positive PCR and toxin. Oral vancomycin was started for a 14-day course. His G-tube was clogged on admission, leading to supplemental nutrition; it was successfully exchanged on hospital day 4. Creatinine rose to 2.4 due to poor oral intake but improved to baseline with IV fluids. Blood pressure remained elevated, prompting initiation of amlodipine. He was discharged home with services to continue tube feeds, complete antibiotics, and follow up with his primary team.
problems: Enterocolitis due to Clostridium difficile, not specified as recurrent
Age-related osteoporosis without current pathological fracture
Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms
Elevated blood-pressure reading, without diagnosis of hypertension

EXAMINATION:  DUPLEX DOPP ABD/PEL

INDICATION:  ___ with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abd pain, sob// ?portal
venous patency, eval of liver, intrabdominal infection pnx

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale, color and spectral Doppler ultrasound images of the
abdomen were obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen pelvis ___, abdominal ultrasound ___, abdominal ultrasound ___

FINDINGS: 

Liver echotexture is normal. There is no evidence of focal liver lesions or
biliary dilatation.
  CHD: 5 mm at the junction of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary
system, and 12 mm inferiorly, similar to prior measurements in ___

There is no ascites, right pleural effusion, or sub- or ___ fluid
collections/hematomas.

The spleen has normal echotexture.
  Spleen length: 10.4 cm

DOPPLER:  The main hepatic arterial waveform is within normal limits, with
prompt systolic upstrokes and continuous antegrade diastolic flow. Peak
systolic velocity in the main hepatic artery is 37.7 cm per second. 
Appropriate arterial waveforms are seen in the anterior right hepatic artery,
posterior write hepatic artery, and the left hepatic artery with resistive
indices of 0.61, 0.66, and 0.69, respectively.  The main portal vein and the
right and left portal veins are patent with hepatopetal flow and normal
waveform.  Appropriate flow is seen in the hepatic veins and the IVC.

IMPRESSION:


1. Patent hepatic vasculature with appropriate waveforms.
2. Mild extrahepatic biliary dilation with common hepatic duct measuring up to
1.2 cm, unchanged compared to prior ultrasound ___.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with GJ tube p/w 3 days of N/V/Abd pain, GJ tube
malpositioned based on CT scan.// please replace GJ tube

COMPARISON:  GJ tube exchange ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ Interventional ___ 
performed the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
50mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 20 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: None
CONTRAST: 30 ml of Optiray contrast
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  3 minutes, 6 mGy

PROCEDURE:  MIC gastrojejunostomy exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

The existing tube was injected with contrast and showed opacification of the
gastric rugae and duodenum.  A stiff Glidewire was introduced into the jejunum
and the tube was removed over-the-wire.  Next a stomal measuring device was
advanced over the wire and the stoma was measured at 2 cm.  A low profile 16
___ 2 cm stomal length mic gastrojejunostomy catheter was advanced over the
wire into position.

The catheters balloon was inflated with 7 ml of contrast contrast diluted in
sterile water in the proximal duodenum and locked in the stomach after
confirming the position of the catheter with a contrast injection. The
catheter was then flushed, capped and secured to the skin with 0-silk sutures.
Sterile dressings were applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Appropriately positioned new 16 ___ MIC 2 cm stomal length low profile
gastrojejunostomy tube.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a gastrojejunostomy tube for a new 16 ___ MIC 2 cm
stomal length low profile gastrojejunostomy tube. The tube is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can I start by confirming your name?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s James. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain and vomiting for the past three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The nurse told me it started around your belly button and feels burning. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It hasn’t moved, but it’s constant. And I’ve thrown up maybe 20 times—mostly just water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel chilly, but I haven’t checked my temperature.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And your stools—have they changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they’ve always been loose because of my colon surgery, but now they’re even more watery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We ran some tests. Your white blood cell count is up, which suggests infection. We also did a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my C. diff again? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on the stool test, but the CT showed something else too. Your feeding tube is coiled back in the stomach and not in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I haven’t been using it much, but my nurse helps me when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely contributing to the nausea and vomiting. We’ll need to fix that. Also, your kidney function is a bit off—your creatinine is 1.5, which is slightly elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s not good. I have CKD, so I worry about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids to help. And we’re starting you on antibiotics for possible C. diff, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oral vancomycin. It’s the best for C. diff. We’ll confirm with the test results tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, James. Your stool test came back positive for C. diff. That explains the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I figured. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history, but we caught it early. You’re on the right treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling a procedure today to replace it. It’s called a GJ tube exchange. It’s quick and done with imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—fentanyl and midazolam—so you’ll be relaxed. The team will monitor you the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi James. The procedure went well. Your new feeding tube is in the right place—down into the jejunum. It’s a low-profile one, so it should be more comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I use it right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s ready. We’ll start with small amounts to make sure you tolerate it. Your nurse will help you manage it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs are improving too. Your bicarbonate was low yesterday—16—which means you were a bit acidic. It’s up to 19 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. And now that your tube is working, we can give you nutrition that way too, which helps balance things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked another stool sample today—still no parasites or other infections. That’s good. It means C. diff is likely the main issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just need to keep taking the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for 10 more days. It’s a 14-day course. Stopping early can cause it to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is back to baseline. Creatinine is 1.4 now. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too, especially with your history. But you’re responding well to fluids and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting in three days, and your appetite is improving. We’re going to try advancing your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with soft foods—like toast and applesauce. If you do well, we’ll move to regular meals by tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the soft diet well. You’re now on a regular diet. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little bloated, but no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your gut is healing. We’ll keep the vancomycin going for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in two days, if all goes well. You’ll need to finish the antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need help with the feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your home nurse already manages your meds and care, so she’ll handle the tube feeds. We’ll send instructions and supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have everything you need. You should follow up with your liver and primary care teams in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. No signs of infection. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot stronger. Can I walk more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We encourage it. Just use your cane if you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge team confirmed home health services will continue. They’ll help with tube feeds and check-ins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your usual meds—tacrolimus, prednisone, loperamide for diarrhea, and your heart meds. We’re not adding anything new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take opium tincture too, for the chronic diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart that as needed, but only after finishing the vancomycin, to avoid interactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved. We’ll get the paperwork ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: finish all the vancomycin, watch for diarrhea returning, and call if you have fever or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see my doctor next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, James.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m all set. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay hydrated, keep using the tube as directed, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One thing—should I avoid any foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-fat, easy-to-digest foods for now—like rice, bananas, toast. Avoid spicy or greasy meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep up with your fluids—especially water and broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You’re all set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, severe malnutrition, and prior colon cancer, was admitted for acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and worsening watery diarrhea. He was found to have C. difficile infection confirmed by positive stool PCR and toxin assay. A CT scan revealed malpositioning of his GJ tube, which was contributing to symptoms. He underwent successful GJ tube exchange and was treated with a 14-day course of oral vancomycin. Acute kidney injury improved with IV fluids, and nutritional support was restored via the new feeding tube. He progressed to a regular diet, remained stable, and was discharged home with instructions to complete antibiotics, resume home nursing care for tube feeds, and follow up with his primary and transplant teams.
